title: Cancer therapy approaches and learning objectives
why: The lecturer welcomes students to the final lecture and introduces the learning objectives regarding cancer treatments and modes of action.

title: Surgery and radiotherapy with adjunctive chemotherapy
why: This section discusses localized physical approaches to cancer treatment, including surgical resection, radiotherapy, and the importance of clean margins and early detection.

title: Cytotoxic chemotherapy: mechanisms, efficacy, toxicity and resistance
why: This section covers classical cytotoxic chemotherapeutic agents, their DNA-damaging mechanisms, clinical efficacy, and major drawbacks such as systemic toxicity and multidrug resistance.

title: Targeting hormone dependence in breast and prostate cancers
why: This section details how hormone-dependent cancers are treated by blocking extracellular signaling receptors using drugs such as tamoxifen and enzalutamide.

title: Exploiting cell cycle checkpoint defects to increase radiosensitivity
why: This section explains strategies to exploit defective cell cycle checkpoints in tumor cells through combination irradiation or p53-selective oncolytic adenoviruses.

title: Oncolytic adenoviruses targeting p53-deficient cancer cells
why: It details how oncolytic adenoviruses lacking E1B 55K selectively replicate in and destroy p53-deficient cancer cells, along with the clinical limitations of this approach.

title: PARP inhibition in BRCA-deficient cancers
why: This section explains synthetic lethality in BRCA-deficient cancers through the use of PARP inhibitors to prevent single-strand DNA break repair.

title: Oncogene addiction and genome-guided targeted therapy
why: This section covers the concept of oncogene addiction and the structural targeting of hyperactivated oncogenic kinases like BCR-ABL, ALK, and EGFR with small molecule inhibitors.

title: Targeting activated oncogenic kinases with ATP-competitive inhibitors
why: The lecturer moves from the general principles of genomic classification and oncogene addiction to the specific mechanisms of kinase hyperactivation and their therapeutic inhibition.

title: Kinase inhibitor selectivity and resistance through binding-site mutations
why: This section addresses the clinical challenges of kinase inhibitors, detailing point mutations, bypass pathways, drug addiction in BRAF-mutant melanoma, and metronomic dosing strategies.

title: BRAF inhibitor resistance, drug addiction and intermittent dosing
why: The passage develops how cancer cells use bypass pathways and paradoxical pathway hyperactivation to resist BRAF V600E targeted therapy, leading to drug addiction and metronomic dosing strategies.

title: Summary of long-term kinase inhibitor treatment and its limitations
why: The lecturer steps back to take stock of kinase inhibitors overall, discussing their transformation of cancer into a chronic condition and remaining side effect challenges.

title: Monoclonal antibodies for receptor blockade and immune-mediated cancer cell killing
why: This section describes therapeutic antibody technologies, including naked monoclonal antibodies targeting surface receptors and antibody-drug conjugates delivering cytotoxic payloads.

title: Antibody–drug conjugates for targeted cytotoxic delivery
why: It explains the mechanism, toxin delivery, and clinical side effects of antibody-drug conjugates using brentuximab as the primary example.

title: Evidence for and against immune surveillance of cancer
why: This section evaluates the evidence for innate cancer immune surveillance through historical transplant studies, immunosuppression outcomes, and adult thymectomy data.

title: Immune checkpoint blockade: T cell reactivation, efficacy and toxicity
why: This section explains how checkpoint inhibitor antibodies like anti-CTLA4 reactivate exhausted T cells, alongside their toxicities and association with tumor mutational burden.

title: Tumor neoantigens and response to immune checkpoint blockade
why: explains what antigens reactivated T cells recognize and how tumor mutational load correlates with immunotherapy response

title: Bispecific T cell engagers in B-cell lymphoma
why: This section covers advanced cellular immunotherapies, detailing the mechanisms, manufacturing challenges, and adverse effects of BiTEs and CAR T cells.

title: CAR T cell therapy: manufacture, limitations and emerging improvements
why: The passage explains chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells as a distinct cell-based immunotherapy modality, covering their engineering process, clinical drawbacks, and ongoing improvements.

title: Summary of cancer therapy challenges and biomarker-guided treatment
why: This section reviews overarching obstacles in cancer treatment, including tumor heterogeneity, whole genome sequencing, historical incidence trends, and future directions.

title: Cancer outcome trends and the contributions of prevention and early detection
why: the lecturer examines whether 50–70 year improvements in cancer outcomes are due to better therapy or rather improved prevention and early detection across various cancer types

title: Future cancer treatment priorities and ethical dilemmas
why: the lecturer explores upcoming frontiers and questions in cancer care, including cancer vaccines, prevention, and palliative care versus continued treatment

title: Lecture close: childhood leukemia survival and the challenge of trialling targeted therapies
why: This section concludes with the success of empirical combination chemotherapy in pediatric leukemia and discusses the clinical dilemma of introducing novel targeted therapies against established cytotoxic regimens.
